title: The Distinction That Could Reshape Super PACs
hook: Citizens United protects unlimited independent spending. Maine's law doesn't touch spending — it caps what one donor may give the committee doing the spending. That gap is now in court.
key_points: A 2024 Maine ballot initiative caps donations to independent-expenditure committees — super PACs — at $5,000; it is being challenged in a federal appeals court.
Lessig's distinction: Buckley and Citizens United protect unlimited independent spending, not unlimited contributions to the spenders.
The only justification the Court has accepted for limiting political money is the risk of corruption.
Super PACs exist because a DC Circuit ruling held that contributions to non-coordinating committees carry no corruption risk.
Lessig points to the bribery allegations against Sen. Robert Menendez — a super PAC contribution as the alleged quid pro quo — as the pattern that ruling deemed impossible; the jury acquitted.
He cites reporting that billionaires supplied 0.3% of outside spending in 2010 and 19% in 2024.
content_html: Campaign finance law rests on a distinction most people never notice. Spending money independently to support a candidate has strong constitutional protection. Contributing money to a candidate can be capped, because a direct gift can buy a favor. Super PACs live in the space between: they make independent expenditures, and the money flowing into them has been treated as untouchable too. Maine voters decided to test that.
extra_html:
A 2024 Maine ballot initiative caps donations to independent-expenditure committees at $5,000, and the law is now before a federal appeals court. Speaking with NPR's Scott Simon, Harvard law professor Lawrence Lessig — who clerked for Justice Scalia, founded Equal Citizens, and helped push the initiative — argues that the law is faithful to Citizens United rather than defiant of it. His reading: the Court in Buckley and again in Citizens United held that independent spending, uncoordinated with a candidate, poses no corruption risk, and corruption risk is the only justification the Court has accepted for limiting political money. Maine's law does not limit anyone's expenditures. It limits the size of contributions into the committees that spend, which Lessig says is a separate question the Court has never squarely resolved.

His evidence that such contributions can corrupt is the bribery case against Senator Robert Menendez, where the alleged quid pro quo ran through a super PAC contribution — precisely the transaction the DC Circuit decision that created super PACs treated as impossible. He notes the jury acquitted, so the pattern is an allegation rather than a proven fact; his point is that the doctrine's factual premise is questionable. He also cites New York Times reporting that billionaires supplied 0.3% of outside spending in 2010, the year super PACs launched, and 19% by 2024, and Brennan Center research finding more than 90% of Americans agree the political system has become corrupted. Lessig is an advocate here, not a neutral analyst, and the appeals court may never reach his theory. But the case is a clean illustration of how doctrinal change usually arrives: not by overruling a famous precedent, but by finding the question it never answered.

related.title: Party Spending & Campaign Finance
related.hook: Since Watergate, a law has capped how much a political party can spend directly coordinating with its own candidate. In 2026 the Supreme Court struck that cap down.

related.title: Interest Groups & Lobbying
related.hook: Between elections, organized groups press their case to government every day. Lobbying is how that pressure is applied — and it's both a feature and a worry of democracy.

related.title: Political Corruption
related.hook: Corruption is the abuse of entrusted power for private gain — and it quietly drains a society, eroding trust, fairness, and the resources meant for everyone.

related.title: Referendums & Direct Democracy
related.hook: Usually we elect others to decide for us. Sometimes the people decide a question themselves — that's direct democracy, and the referendum is its main modern tool.

flashcards.prompt: What is the legal distinction Maine's super PAC law depends on?
flashcards.back_html: Between spending and contributing. The Court has protected unlimited independent expenditures; Maine limits how much one donor may give to the committee that makes those expenditures.

flashcards.prompt: What is the only rationale the Supreme Court has accepted for limiting political money?

choices.text: Equalizing the influence of rich and poor citizens
Reducing the total volume of political advertising

flashcards.explanation_html: Equalizing influence has been rejected as a justification. Because corruption is the accepted rationale, both sides argue over whether super PAC contributions create corruption risk.

flashcards.prompt: Why does Lessig treat the Menendez case as important even though the jury acquitted?

choices.text: Because the alleged pattern — a favor traded for a super PAC contribution — is what the ruling creating super PACs said could not happen
Because the acquittal overturned Citizens United
Because it was the first case to define independent expenditures

flashcards.explanation_html: His argument is about the factual premise of the doctrine: if such a quid pro quo is even plausible enough to charge, the assumption that these contributions pose no corruption risk is shaky.
